newsitem.title: UK: Dollar buoyed vs mark, yen before U.S. jobs data.
newsitem.headline: Dollar buoyed vs mark, yen before U.S. jobs data.

text.p: The dollar topped 119 yen for the first time in 11 weeks and was bobbing below Monday's seven-and-a-half-year peak against the mark with traders looking to the July U.S. jobs data later on Friday for a cue to push it higher.
Optimism about the dollar's prospects resurfaced after U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated on Thursday that a strong dollar is in America's interests.

His comments reassured traders that a stronger dollar was not about to reignite trade tensions between the U.S. and Japan. It also assured them that the U.S. will not back Bundesbank calls for an end to the dollar's rally against the mark.
Confirmation from the U.S. non-farm payrolls report at 1230 GMT that the U.S. economy is expanding without stoking inflation is expected by analysts to bolster the dollar further.

"The dollar has been going up and down like a cork in water but got some support from Rubin's comments overnight," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "U.S. markets seem to be on a roll for the time being and the dollar is likely to trend with the bond market after the jobs report."
The dollar climbed to 119.17 yen, the strongest it has been since May 13. It was last at 119.10/20 from 118.33/38 late Thursday in Europe.
Dollar/mark was at 1.8462/67, up from 1.8395/05 yesterday and a third of a pfennig below Monday's high of 1.8490.

The dollar's 6.3 percent surge against the mark in July has encountered resistance from the Bundesbank, which has floated the possibility it could use variable-rate tenders to nudge its securities repurchase rate up from a record low of 3.0 percent.

Meantime, an official from Japan's Automobile Manufacturers' Association said on Thursday he did not want a weaker yen because of the implications for Japan's trade relations. The dollar's rise to 57-month highs against the yen in May eroded U.S. competitiveness and elicited complaints from its exporters.
While the dollar has retreated nearly 7 percent from these peaks, U.S. automakers still think it is too expensive.
Andrew Card, the president of the American Automobile Association, said on Thursday the yen was too weak against the dollar and should trade in a range of 95 to 100.
As long as the U.S. administration does not back these calls, though, traders will be happy to drive the dollar higher, analysts said.
"The general feeling is that we are still in an uptrend and that dollar/mark will hit new highs," said Craig Justham, deputy manager of foreign exchange at Creditanstalt Bankverein here.
Concern that German interest rates could tick up is also beginning to fade, paving the way for another test of the psychologically important 1.85-mark level, analysts said.
"German rate fears have been consigned to the back burner for the time being," said Coleman at CIBC.
This, together with revived speculation that UK interest rates could rise next week from 6.75 percent, helped sterling to claw back ground against the mark.
The pound was at 3.0260/70 marks from 3.0130/40 late Thursday in Europe.
